results.title: Lateral group transfer question
results.query:
Lateral group transfer question: In the General Vol 21 Number 1 scenario A series replay, on turn 5 the American plays a sideways movement card on his group C "as a Lateral Group Transfer". But given the German player only has groups at identity chit A and B isn't this illegal? Rule 17.7 first sentence says "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

The rule states the player announces the intention to perform a lateral group transfer so presumably if the player doesn't make the announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways he can't subsequently do so on a future turn (using that same played movement card) even if the necessary conditions still exist to make such a move? 

Where a game is played without aid of voice or text chat I guess you might agree that a lateral group transfer announcement was accompanied by putting down the new group identity chit in the adjacent column and taken away if the attempt failed.

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

Edit: Looking through past posts I see I have broached this issue before! See https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1342845/article/35597336#35597336 where no conclusion was reached :)
results.generated_answer:
Verdict: CONDITIONAL

Ruling: According to Rule 17.7, a Lateral Group Transfer can only occur if there is no other friendly group in that position at the start of the turn and the group must be directly opposite an opposing group. In the given scenario, if the American player attempts a Lateral Group Transfer with Group C to an adjacent column where there are no other friendly groups and is directly opposite a German group, the transfer would be legal. 

However, if the German player only has groups at identity chits A and B, and there is no open position for the American Group C to transfer to that is directly opposite a German group, the transfer would be illegal.

Regarding the announcement of the Lateral Group Transfer, Rule 17.7 requires the player to announce the intention to perform a lateral group transfer. If the player does not make this announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways, they cannot subsequently do so on a future turn using that same played movement card, even if the necessary conditions still exist.

As for changing one's mind after declaring the intention to perform a Lateral Group Transfer, there is no explicit rule addressing this situation. However, given the requirement for an announcement and the potential for opponents to react to this announcement (e.g., by playing terrain cards), it would be against the spirit of the game to allow a player to change their mind after declaring a Lateral Group Transfer. Therefore, once a player has announced their intention to perform a Lateral Group Transfer, they should be committed to attempting that transfer.
results.ground_truth_answer:
In the General Vol 21 Number 1 scenario A series replay, on turn 5 the American plays a sideways movement card on his group C "as a Lateral Group Transfer". But given the German player only has groups at identity chit A and B isn't this illegal? Rule 17.7 first sentence says "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

No, it says "A group capable of movement can change its group identity and thereby its position directly opposing an enemy group...."  All it is saying if you move group from B to C, the directly opposing group would now be C--if it exists.  If the opponent  does not have a Group C, then there would be no directly opposing group to your Group C.  (Just like there would be if each side set up with a different number of groups at start.)

It is not stating a requirement, but a change of status of "directly opposing" groups.

The rule states the player announces the intention to perform a lateral group transfer so presumably if the player doesn't make the announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways he can't subsequently do so on a future turn (using that same played movement card) even if the necessary conditions still exist to make such a move? 

Correct, if the intention to change a group's ID is not made when playing the movement cards, when group enters terrain, the same Group ID remains.  Very common if you want to get into better terrain.

Where a game is played without aid of voice or text chat I guess you might agree that a lateral group transfer announcement was accompanied by putting down the new group identity chit in the adjacent column and taken away if the attempt failed.

A common technique in ftf play is to place the new ID on the Movement card until new terrain is accepted or rejected (which would cancel the transfer).

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

I would say no per errata on Rule 5:  Movement cards not played directly to the discard pile cannot voluntarily be cancelled.  (Just like you can't rotate a Movement card from advancing to sideways because you change your mind about advancing.)

No big deal, that thread started 11 years ago and you added your question 5 years after that.

results.title: AFV questions (stun effect, etc.)
results.query:
AFV questions (stun effect, etc.): Background:  I have been playing Up Front for over 40 years, but I never liked AFV's and so avoided them.  Now I'm trying to use them more, and this has raised some questions that I didn't have to think about before.

Is a stunned, non-OT AFV forced to button up?  I think I had always assumed the answer was "yes", but re-reading the rules yesterday, I wasn't sure.  The clearest rule I can find is 28.45, which says, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side."

Well, that is ambiguous.  It says it's only referring to CE AFVs, but then it mentions a Buttoned Up side, which a CE AFV does not have.  I think on the whole that I would find it odd that regular AFV's don't button up when stunned when OT AFV's do, but that's not much of a guide to go on.

I'd like to follow this up with a dumb question about boxed attacks.  I'm pretty sure I understand them, but they seem weird, so I just wanted to verify.  In brief:  when you shoot a boxed effect number against an AFV, you know exactly what's going to happen if you hit.  You simply add your boxed number to your relative range, and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.  (There are exceptions for rifleman using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW.)  This feels weird to me because everything else in Up Front is accompanied by massive amounts of randomness, so for a hit's result to be absolutely known (with the possible exception of an immobilization or stun in case they have the same effect number) seems incongruous.  I just want to make sure I'm getting it right.
results.generated_answer:
Verdict: CONDITIONAL

Ruling:
1. **Stunned AFV Button Up Status**:
   - [Rule 28.45] states, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side." This rule explicitly refers to CE AFVs. 
   - However, the rule's mention of a "Buttoned Up side" is ambiguous because CE AFVs do not have a Buttoned Up side. 
   - Given the context and the intention behind the rule, it is reasonable to infer that a stunned, non-OT AFV should button up, aligning with the behavior of OT AFVs when stunned. 
   - Therefore, a stunned, non-OT AFV is **CONDITIONALLY** required to button up, based on the interpretation of the rule's intent.

2. **Boxed Attacks Against AFVs**:
   - [Rule 28.4] explains that when attacking an AFV with a boxed effect number, the result is determined by comparing the attack's final result number to the AFV's defense values.
   - This process is indeed less random compared to other attacks in Up Front, as the outcome is known once the attack hits.
   - Your understanding of boxed attacks is correct: you add your boxed number to your relative range and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.
   - Exceptions exist for riflemen using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW, as noted in the rule.
   - Thus, your interpretation of boxed attacks is accurate, though it does introduce a degree of certainty not typically seen in other Up Front mechanics.
results.ground_truth_answer:
Couple of things - about getting AFVs to button up, one way for infantry to reduce the threat of an AFV is to fire at it with small arms, hoping to get a hit equal to or higher than its Morale value, which forces it to button up.  This is covered by 28.3:

An AFV card has two Armor defense values printed on each side of the card plus a Morale and CE Defense value on the front of the card. The Armor and Flank defense values represent the armored defense strength and is listed on both sides of the card; only attacks using solely boxed firepower or boxed "Effect Numbers" apply to this value. The MORALE and CE values are affected only by unboxed attack values.

This is how mortars can attack AFVs (and they have a small chance of damaging the vehicle as well [26.5]).  AT guns have the choice of firing AP - the process the OP referred to in his second question, which attacks the Armor/Flank values - or HE, which attacks the Morale value as above.  The HE attack is only possible, of course, when the vehicle is CE, or in the case of an OT vehicle if it is not already Pinned (except for one or two really weedy AFVs like the British Bren Carrier, which has a Panic value and can thus be attacked when Pinned).

And moving on to the OPs second question, you were right to feel that there should be a random element is resolving an AP hit - and there is!  25.4 says:

Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.)  The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5]. 

So the Hit process establishes first whether a hit has been obtained, and secondly how damaging it is: for HE, the RNC on the To Hit card is used (provided a 0 would have hit, reflecting how close the HE round actually landed), and for AP a hit is a hit, but the RR is added to reflect increased penetration at closer ranges.  This gives you the base hit strength; then, in both cases, you draw an RNC for each target.  Firing at an AFV, of course, there is only one target, but you still draw an RNC.

So, a Panther (s7,i8,k9) rumbles up to RR4 to a plucky British 6-pdr (FE 3).  If the AT gun gets a hit, its base Hit Strength will be 3+4=7, and then it hopes the RNC will be at least 0, and preferably a black 2 or better to get a kill.

Don't forget, also, that unlike small arms and HE fire against an AFV, terrain does affect the resolution.  So if the AFV is in Brush, the Hit Strength is reduced by 1.  I suppose this reflects the possibility of the round being deflected or slowed by intervening obstacles.

Hope all that helps!  Oh, and Snipers are good, too.

results.title: Rules don't explicitly tell you when you lose Natural Flanking Fire?
results.query:
Rules don't explicitly tell you when you lose Natural Flanking Fire?: I imagine it's as simple as you are no longer in the conditions for it and therefore don't have it.  The 17.4 section only refers to Flanking Fire.  It's specifying that specific rule.  Not the Natural one as far as I can tell.  

FF is lost when the flanking group plays a movement but that would be an odd condition for NFF since it wouldn't necessarily break the conditions needed for NFF.  I guess then can a group currently at NFF play, say, a lateral movement card, thereby not changing range chit, thereby maintaining the conditions for NFF and still enjoy the benefits of double fire power?  Which now has me remembering discussions on do you double first or halve first and if halve first do you still round down before doubling.... 

Wait a minute... upon further inspection... 17.3 (NFF) still speicifcally calls it Flanking Fire.  So the 17.4 losing conditions do apply to NFF?  Removing wire and failing to Ford a stream would make you lose NFF?  But how would one regain NFF as you're still in the exact same conditions to qualify for it?  But... the condition for NFF is moving forward to RR4 (chits 6) from RR5.  That seems to be it.  Moving forward.  So stopping at RR4 (6 on chits) you lose it as you no longer are moving? I know over thinking it but...
results.generated_answer:
Verdict: CONDITIONAL

Ruling: Natural Flanking Fire (NFF) is a specific instance of Flanking Fire that occurs when a group moves forward to Relative Range 4 from Relative Range 5, placing it behind an adjacent enemy group which also has an opposing group directly in front of it [Rule 17.3]. 

The conditions for losing Flanking Fire, as specified in Rule 17.4, apply to all forms of Flanking Fire, including NFF. Therefore, actions such as playing a Movement card, removing Wire, or failing to ford a Stream would cause a group to lose NFF [Rule 17.41, 17.43].

Regaining NFF requires the group to again move forward to Relative Range 4 from Relative Range 5, reestablishing the conditions specified in Rule 17.3. Simply playing a lateral movement card without changing range would not maintain NFF, as the condition requires forward movement to Relative Range 4 [Rule 17.3].

In summary, NFF is lost when the conditions that established it are no longer met, specifically when the group is no longer moving forward to Relative Range 4 from Relative Range 5. It can be regained by again satisfying those conditions.
results.ground_truth_answer:
Flanking is a complicated rule.

Gaining Natural Flanking is a result of moving from RR5 to "RR6" per 17.3.. (I prefer "RR6" to "RR4 but behind the target group".)

Losing any form of Flanking occurs under 17.4X, specifically:
-  Flanking group has a movement or Wire played on it.  (but not Terrain--needed to get doubled FP without 1/2FP for moving.)
-  Flanked group has terrain, even if rejected.
-  Flanked group has a Movement played on it, even temporarily to remove Wire or failed Ford attempt.
-  Front group eliminated or changes ID chit/completes a lateral group "transfer".

Gaining flanking (either naturally or via a Flank card) places a Flank Fire chit.  Losing Flanking removes the Flank Fire chit.  The presence of the ***chit*** determines doubled FP for flanking.

Once, natural flanking is lost  it would be difficult to regain. (retreat to RR5 and advance back to RR6) But, when in a natural Flanking position (i.e. RR6) (whether Flanking was lost or not), that group can Encircle on a later turn (if the Front group is at RR2 to the Flanked group), by playing a sideways Movement cards on the Flanking group.

And always double/halve all FP before rounding down.

The point of the rule is you have only have the right to retarget a sniper or Minefield if it's target group ends up empty before resolution.  You cannot do that with other active discards (Terrain, Wire)

results.title: Clarification on split action cards and nationality markings
results.query:
Clarification on split action cards and nationality markings: Re-reading the rules, I noticed something that I think I "learned" incorrectly years ago, when there's two possible actions on a split action card.  The image serves to illustrate my question.   

Q:   Do nationality markings refer to everything on that side of the card?    In particular, when nationality markings are along the side of the card where it says Radio.  

The card on the left I had long interpreted to mean any nation could use it as a Rally card, but only the American or Russian player could use it for the Radio.  But re-reading the rules, now I think that only the American or Russian can use the card at all, for either Rally or Radio. 

The middle card same thing, the Russian can use Concealment, and the American or German can use it for Rally or Radio.

The right-hand card is easiest to understand, it's a Cower card for the Americans and a Rally card for the Germans or Russians.
results.generated_answer:
Verdict: CONDITIONAL

Ruling:
According to [Rule 2.21], split action cards are divided into two parts, each specifying different actions by nationality. A player may only use the action listed on their side of the card as indicated by the nationality symbol(s) printed on that side of the card. 

Applying this to your specific questions:

1. For the left-hand card, if the nationality symbols (American and Russian) are next to the "Radio" action, then only the American or Russian player can use the card for either "Rally" or "Radio." Other nationalities cannot use this card at all.

2. For the middle card, if the nationality symbols (American and German) are next to the "Rally" and "Radio" actions, then only the American or German player can use the card for either "Rally" or "Radio." The Russian player can only use it for "Concealment."

3. For the right-hand card, if there are no nationality symbols next to the "Cower" action for Americans, then it is a Cower card for Americans. The "Rally" action with German and Russian symbols means only Germans or Russians can use it for "Rally."

Thus, the interpretation depends on the exact placement of the nationality symbols relative to the actions on the card.
results.ground_truth_answer:
If the card is a Split Action card with RADIO, then only the nationalities indicated on that side can use the card as RADIO or RALLY (because all RADIO cards are paired with rallies).

If the card is NOT  a split action card, but has nationality indicators next to RADIO, any nationality can use the card to Rally, but only the indicated nationalities can use the RADIO.

Also of course, Japanese use Russian Split Action, French use German and British use either German or American except for a RADIO which must be both German AND American.  Italian use no Split Actions (unless elite).

The key point here is that the reduction in attack strength due to a malfunction is based on the original firepower of the weapon before any doubling effects are applied. Therefore, the attack strength would be reduced by 3, not 5, because the LMG's original firepower was 5, not 10.

Thus, the attack is reduced by 3 when the LMG malfunctions. [Rule 19.13]
results.ground_truth_answer:

results.title: Does a group directly opposite to a Banzai declaration, that decreases its range chit, permit Banzai cancellation?
results.query:
Does a group directly opposite to a Banzai declaration, that decreases its range chit, permit Banzai cancellation?: Hello everyone,

Given this section of rule 45.43:
"The Japanese player has the option to cancel a 
Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no 
longer directly opposite or adjacent), "

Situation: A group declares Banzai on a directly opposite group at RR 1. The target group of the Banzai retrograde moves and decreases its range chit from 1 to 0.
Does the Banzai group have the option to cancel the Banzai? 

I am not sure if the "out of range" and parenthetical section applies to both parts of the "or"

Thanks,

John
results.generated_answer:
Verdict: CONDITIONAL

Ruling:
According to Rule 45.43, a Banzai attack can be cancelled if the target group "retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no longer directly opposite or adjacent)."

In the given situation, the target group decreases its range chit from 1 to 0 by retrograde movement. This movement does not make the target group "no longer directly opposite or adjacent," as it remains directly opposite the Banzai group. Therefore, the condition for cancellation based on the target group no longer being directly opposite or adjacent is not met.

However, the rule also states that a Banzai attack can be cancelled if the target group "moves laterally out of range." The retrograde movement in this case is not a lateral movement, so this condition is also not met.

Therefore, the Banzai group does not have the option to cancel the Banzai attack based on the provided scenario.

[Rule 45.43]
results.ground_truth_answer:
No.  Simply retreating does not allow the Japanese to cancel Banzai.  But retreating (or moving laterally or having another group moving) to a positon where Banzai could not have been declared.  The "out of range" wording is really terrible.

Moving laterally is easy to explain.  Japanese Group A declares Banzai on American Group B.  Then the targetted American Group moves laterally moves to C--then the targeted group is now "out of range" (i.e. no longer directly opposite or adjacent.) so now the Japanese could cancel the Banzai.

As for retreating causing a Banzai group to be no longer eligible to be Banzaied, you have to check the errata.
Per the errata, 45.4 should have inserted after the third sentence, "However, Banzai may not be declared against an enemy group that is blocked at the time Banzai is declared."  
 It gives an example (modified slightly to make better example for this question).

AM:  A(3)  B(2)
JP:  A(0)  B(0)
The Japanese player cannot have Group A declare Banzai against American Group B, because direct movement of Japan A to American B to RR5 is not possible since it is blocked by American A.

What happens if a targetted group retreats into a blocked position, like this:

AM:  A(3)  B(3)
JP:  A(0)  B(0)

Japan A declares Banzai on American B, then Anerican B retreats to RC 2 and is now in a blocked position (like above).  Now, the Japanese Group A can cancel the Banzai, because now Banzaiing Japan group A is blocked from targetted American Group B by American Group A.

What happens if American A moves forward to RC4 after Japan A declared Banzai on American B in this position.  The same thing!  Banzai Japan A is blocked from tragetted American B by American A.

The sentence from Rule 45.43 quoted in the original question is incomplete.  In full it reads:
The Japanese player has the option to cancel a Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no longer directly opposite or adjacent),  or if another enemy moves in such a way as to block the access of the Banzai group to the declared target.

The missing text covers this third situation.

The Japanese are allowed to cancel a Banzai only if a position arises where it would not be legal to declare it.  This also prevents a Banzaiing group from attacking a different enemy group than the one it is targetting (which never mentioned in the rules or errata--given the blocking rules, obviously is not allowed.)

Hope this helps.

results.title: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
results.query: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
results.generated_answer:
Verdict: PROHIBITED

Ruling:
According to Rule 17.7, a Lateral Group Transfer requires the play of a Movement card in the sideways mode and the subsequent play of a Terrain card to complete the transfer. The rule explicitly states that the group identity change does not occur until a Terrain card is played on the sideways Movement card and accepted. 

However, the rule does not allow for the discarding of terrain on a Lateral Group Transfer. The process of a Lateral Group Transfer is distinct from the normal process of discarding terrain to change a group's terrain, as outlined in Rule 5.3 and Rule 7.31. 

Therefore, terrain cannot be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer. The transfer is only completed by playing and accepting a Terrain card, not by discarding terrain.
results.ground_truth_answer:
Ok. So say it's just one man doing a lateral group transfer leaving a group that is in a building for a group in another building. My opponent drops a stream on my guy. Is he now alone in the stream? Does he become his own group? Is the group that he left now in a stream as well? What's going on here?

You seem to be confusing Lateral Group Transfer with Individual Transfer.  The rules are unnecessarily confusing with calling both very different actions "transfers".

Lateral Group Transfer (17.7) = lateral movement of a group from Group B to Group C (for example).  (This should be called "Lateral Movement".)  This is initiated by playing a Movement card in sideways mode while declaring the Lateral Movement.  (I generally put the new group marker on the movement card).  Prerequisite:  there can be no group ID in the location that you are going to (unless you are switching positions of two groups--which I won't get into here.)  On a later turn, the Transf...I mean Lateral Movement is completed by playing terrain on the group (The Group ID applies only now.)  The Lateral Movement is cancelled if terrain discarded by opponent is rejected or if open ground played under Wire that was played on the Laterally Moving group (as either would remove sideways Movement card.)

Individual Transfer (17.8) is transferring Individual men between groups.  First, the groups must be adjacent and at the same range chit and one or both groups must have an unpinned leader.  Then, one Movement card is played for each transferring man (more than one man can transfer.) and a Transfer chit on the man.  Transfer is completed when the receiving group uses an action to accept the transferring men (which can be placed in any position in their new group). I thought i knew this game but maybe i do not.

So If an attack gets the exact number equal to KIA value of an unpinned personality card (lets say an eight), then that card is not KIA is the wound column is equal to printed morale value. 

If the final fire resolution number (i.e. including the RNC for the man) exactly equals the KIA # then you check RPC7w and if RPC7w equals the morale value of the man, the man will be wounded instead of KIA.  This happens whether the target man was pinned or not and he will retain his (un)pinned status.

But also lets say you have a pinned card and attack it is equal to greater than the panic number so you check the rout number and the rnc rout column says it routs  instead fo panic but also the wound column matches the morale, that card does not panic, does not route but instead is wounded. Rule 33.1 Wounds states that wounds "may possibly occur anytime an infantryman **routs** or otherwise be eliminated by a KIA result as a result of an RNC generating a final attack strength exactly equal to the lowest number required for KIA."  This would require a wound check on RPC7 when the pinned man routs as well.

To summarize:
On a pinned man:
- if the Fire Resolution number (FRN) > KIA, the man is dead.  No wound check is made.
-  if the FRN = KIA (usually 9), check for wound
-  if FRN < KIA but >= PANIC, first check RPC0r determine ROUT/KIA.

-  if RPC0r > Rout #, the man likely routs, but check for wound first.
- if RPC0r <= Rout #, the man is KIA. No wound check.

Yes.  Malfunction rules are some of the most confusing in the game.  Pretty much you have to follow the errata exclusively.

This is a legacy from Squad Leader's malfunction rules.  Roll the worst natural number and weapon breaks--but only weapons on separate counters were affected--not every rifle which were intrinsic to each squad counter.

19.11 says "If the firing group contains only one firing weapon with usable firepower factors, and a red RNC is drawn to resolve its attack that weapon automatically malfunctions..."

No, it says "Red 6 RNC", though technically that isn't correct.  It should be "Red RNC drawn that causes a malfunction."  This makes a difference with uncrewed machine guns (and Japanese and Italian LMGs) which have a malfunction number of x5-6.

Basically, that sentence is telling you no RPC is needed to determine which weapon broke--because there's only one.  The next clause of that rule states the attack terminates when this happens and no further men in the target group need be resolved.

So, question no. 1: If I have a German group containing only a single personality card:  #4 with a Bolt-Action rifle. If this group fires and the RNC is a red 2, will Pvt. Schumacher's Mauser malfunction automatically?

No, because the rifle breaks on a Red 6.  If it were Red 6, then the rifle would malfunction and it would end the attack.

Question no. 2: If this group instead was a German group consisting of two personality cards: #1 with a Machine Pistol which is assisting crew to #3 with an LMG. And the RNC is a red 2, will the Pfc. Schüssel's MG 34 automatically malfunction?

How many men are  is in this group?  I count three:
1)  a machine Pistol as a crewman for
2)  an LMG
3)  a rifleman

I am going to assume three men for this explanation.  (All unpinned)  I have my reasons.

If a Red 6 RNC is drawn, all three are considered firing and are subject to malfunction, an RPC(3) is drawn per 19.13 per errata:
-  On a 1, the crewman is affected, no malfunction occurs and the attack continues with -1 to Fire Strength for the remaining men for a momentary belt bobble.
-  On a 2, the LMG is affected.  The weapon malfs and the attack continues with the Fire Strength reduced by 1/2 the firepower (round up) provided by the LMG at this range for the remaining men.
-  On a 3, the rifle is affected.  However, at RR0 it provides no firepower (but it is STILL considered "firing") so the rifle malfunctions and there is no effect on fire strength on the attack.  At any other range, it is providing FP, the rifle Is malfed and the rest of the attack is resolved reducing the FS by 1/2 FP provided by the rifle (round up).

Now let's say the crewman and the rifleman were pinned (Only the LMG is unpinned.  STILL all three are considered "firing").  If a Red 6 RNC is drawn, all three could be affected, but if the RPC(3) chooses a pinned man (either the crewman or rifleman) then the weapon simply breaks with no effect on FS for the rest of the attack, because a pinned man was chosen.  If the LMG were selected, the normal penalties apply.

However, if a Red 5 RNC were drawn, the only weapon that could be affected is the now uncrewed LMG ( see 11.1).  (Uncrewed LMGs malf on x5-6.  The MP and rifle malf on x6.) In this case, no RPC is required and the LMG automatically breaks with the normal penalties.

Yes, it confusing.  Stick to the errata on all malfunction rules.

Bottom line, does this halftrack become vulnerable to a lot more Fire cards when it plays a move card in sideways mode? 

EDIT: The clause in question that is confusing me is,” In addition to normal Flanking Fire opportunities, an AFV is subject to a Flank Shot whenever it has a Movement card in play in the sideways mode.” (From 28.46) Further down, from 28.51, “An AFV in Woods can leave that Terrain card only by playing a Movement card in the sideways mode.” I have posted about a halftrack, but this question does apply to closed top AFVs as well, if they are not Buttoned Up. When playing today, I wanted to try playing a Woods card on a moving halftrack to make my groups in flanking locations eligible for Flanking Fire with big FP cards at the halftrack’s Morale 5 and CE 9. Still unsure if that would have been legal.

Ruling:
According to Rule 28.46, an AFV is subject to a Flank Shot whenever it has a Movement card in play in the sideways mode. This means that the AFV exposes its side armor and must defend with its FLANK defense values instead of its normal ARMOR defense values. However, the rule specifically refers to ordnance fire enjoying a Flanking Fire advantage.

Regarding Flanking Fire, Rule 17.3 describes Natural Flanking Fire, which occurs when a group moves forward to Relative Range 4 from Relative Range 5, placing it behind an adjacent enemy group. This is different from the Flank Shot described in 28.46.

In the scenario provided, the Halftrack in group B moves sideways with a flank move card to flank opponent’s group C. According to Rule 28.46, the Halftrack is subject to a Flank Shot, meaning it must use its FLANK defense values against ordnance fire. However, this does not automatically grant eligible opposing groups (A and C) Flanking Fire with big FP Fire cards. Flanking Fire, as described in Rule 17.3, is a separate condition that depends on the relative ranges and positions of the groups, not merely the sideways movement of the AFV.

Therefore, the Halftrack becomes vulnerable to ordnance fire with its FLANK defense values due to the sideways move, but it does not automatically become vulnerable to Flanking Fire from groups A and C unless the conditions of Rule 17.3 are also met.
results.ground_truth_answer:
AH uses "Flank" in two different ways:  Flanking Fire and Flank boxed defense values.  (They really should have called the latter "Side defense values" or something similar.)

Basically the AFV uses Flank defense values when:
-  The AFV is moving in sideways mode.
-  AFV being flanked by the enemy.
-  Bogged or Immobilized.

If an AFV has a sideways Flank Movement in play, then they would use Flank defense values due to moving sideways, but once the AFV enters terrain, it still retains the Flank Fire chit (and doubled FP.), but no longer uses the Flank defense values.

Note further, Armor and Flank defense values are only used when being attacked by boxed ordnance or boxed FP (FTs, minefields, RR5 1 boxed FP per weapon (but only if the AFV is open topped, 28.7) )

results.ground_truth_answer:
Two key rules here:
7.2. This rule specifies that if the top.card on a group is a movement card, then only  the next movement or terrain card applies.
13.1. Smoke (and wire) modifies the last terrain card played.  (At the beginning of the game, lack of a terrain card = open ground.)

Note:  the rule 13.1 does NOT say Smoke modifies Movement cards, only the last terrain card played.  That would mean if  two movement cards are in play on a group, any Smoke modifies the prior terrain, but that terrain would not count per 7.2.

But examples B & C  under rule 13.25 clearly contradicts this.  (Far from the only place where AH effectively vetoed a rule with an example.)  Given other situations discovered before, I am assuming the example is what AH intended.

So it should be played as any Smoke under 2 or more Movement cards is ignored (per example C as the Smoke modified a terrain card (or virtual Open Ground) which no longer counts.) But any Smoke above the second Movement card (in a stack with 2 or more movement cards) is counted (per example B, but I'm not sure of the terrain being modified....)

That being said, Smoke is rarely played while a group is moving.  It is usually played before you start moving a group, then move the group, then place the group in terrain.  

If you must Move twice (desperate times can require desperate measures), using an extra turn to play the Smoke after the first Movement card provides little extra cover (which might get blown away) at the additional chance for the opponent to fire at the group or put it in Wire or a Stream.
